lessonTitle: Recognition and Response: Vital Signs, Track-and-Trigger, SBAR and First-Line Treatment

blocks.text: A 55-year-old man on a medical ward has been 'a bit sleepy' since lunchtime. Each observation set looks only a little abnormal, and nobody has been worried. But the pattern across six hours shows a rising respiratory rate and a falling blood pressure. Many in-hospital cardiac arrests are preceded by hours of recorded warning signs, and recognising them is the job of whoever picks up the chart.

blocks.markdown: **Vital signs** (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, temperature and level of consciousness) are the body's simplest measures of whether oxygen is being taken up and delivered. **Trends matter more than a single value**: a respiratory rate that moves from 16 to 24 over a few hours is more worrying than a stable 22. Respiratory rate is often the earliest sign of deterioration yet is the least accurately recorded, so count it for a full minute when it matters. Blood pressure is a late sign, because young and fit patients compensate by raising their pulse and vasoconstricting until they suddenly decompensate.

blocks.title: Track-and-trigger system
blocks.text: A scheme that scores routine vital signs against pre-set bands and links the total score, or a single extreme value, to a defined level of clinical response. In England, NEWS2 (the National Early Warning Score 2, from the Royal College of Physicians) is the commonly used tool. Always check the chart and thresholds that apply in your trust.

blocks.caption: NEWS2 scoring bands (scale 1 saturations). Verify against the current Royal College of Physicians chart; scale 2 applies only where a clinician has set a target of 88 to 92 percent.

blocks.markdown: Add the item scores to give the aggregate. The usual response bands are: **0 to 4 low**, **5 to 6 medium** (urgent response), **7 or more high** (emergency response), and a **single parameter scoring 3** also triggers an urgent review. Remember that these are minimum triggers: if you are worried, escalate regardless of the score. Two further tools help interpret the picture. **Mean arterial pressure (MAP)** estimates the average perfusion pressure over the cardiac cycle. The **qSOFA** prompt (from the Sepsis-3 consensus) counts three bedside features, namely respiratory rate 22 per minute or more, altered mentation and systolic BP 100 mmHg or less, and a score of 2 or more flags higher risk of a poor outcome in suspected infection; it is a prompt to think, not a diagnosis, and current NICE guidance should be checked for which tool your trust uses.

blocks.caption: Approximate mean arterial pressure in mmHg; SBP is systolic and DBP is diastolic blood pressure.

blocks.title: Interpreting a sick patient's observations
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old man admitted with a urinary tract infection has: respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 95 percent on air, BP 96/52 mmHg, pulse 118 per minute, new confusion, temperature 39.3 degrees Celsius. Calculate the NEWS2 aggregate, the MAP and the qSOFA count, and interpret them.

steps.text: Score NEWS2 item by item: respiratory rate 24 scores 2, SpO2 95 percent scores 1, air scores 0, systolic BP 96 scores 2, pulse 118 scores 2, new confusion scores 3, temperature 39.3 scores 2.
Calculate the MAP with SBP 96 and DBP 52.

Count qSOFA: respiratory rate of 24 meets the 22 or more criterion, new confusion is altered mentation, and a systolic BP of 96 is 100 mmHg or less, so all three criteria are met and the qSOFA count is 3.

Interpret: an aggregate of 12 is in the high band and needs an emergency response. With fever, tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion on a background of urinary infection, this is suspected septic shock physiology. Call for senior help immediately and start first-line treatment.

blocks.answer: NEWS2 = 12 (high risk), MAP about 67 mmHg, qSOFA = 3: emergency escalation and treatment of suspected sepsis.

blocks.title: Reassuring numbers can mislead
blocks.text: A normal pulse does not exclude shock in a patient on a beta-blocker or with a pacemaker, a young adult can look well until late, and a patient with chronic lung disease may have a lower baseline saturation. Interpret the numbers against the patient, the trend and your clinical impression.

blocks.markdown: **Structured communication with SBAR.** SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation. Situation is who you are, which patient and the current problem. Background gives the admission diagnosis, relevant history and treatment so far. Assessment gives the latest observations, early warning score, findings and your impression of the severity. Recommendation states what you want and by when. The tool prevents rambling and makes sure the listener hears the most important item, which is the request. Have the observations, drug chart and notes ready before you phone, and finish by confirming the plan back.

blocks.title: An SBAR for the patient above
blocks.prompt: Write the SBAR you would give the medical registrar for the 55-year-old man in the previous example, after you have examined him and started first-line treatment.

steps.text: Situation: 'This is Dr A, the F1 on the medical ward. I am calling about Mr B, a 55-year-old man whose NEWS2 is 12 with hypotension and new confusion.'

Background: 'He was admitted yesterday with a urinary tract infection and is on ward-based antibiotics. He has no known allergies that I have recorded and no beta-blocker. He is for full escalation at present.'

Assessment: 'Respiratory rate 24, SpO2 95 percent on air, BP 96/52, pulse 118, temperature 39.3, new confusion. I think he is in septic shock from a urinary source. I have started oxygen, taken blood cultures and a lactate, and started a fluid bolus.'
Recommendation: 'Please can you come and review him within the next 15 minutes? I would like your advice about broad-spectrum antibiotics, ongoing fluid and whether to call critical care outreach.'
Close the loop: repeat the agreed plan and time of review, then write the time, name of the person and the plan in the notes.

blocks.answer: A good SBAR is concise, uses the numbers, states the impression and ends with a specific request and time frame; the plan is repeated back and documented.

blocks.markdown: **First-line treatment while awaiting help.** For any acutely unwell patient the ABCDE approach tells you what to fix first. Treat problems as you find them: open the airway, give oxygen as the target range dictates (high-concentration oxygen through a reservoir mask is a common initial step in a critically ill patient, then titrate to a target saturation of 94 to 98 percent, or 88 to 92 percent where hypercapnia is a risk), obtain intravenous access and take bloods including a blood gas or lactate, give intravenous fluid for hypovolaemia or sepsis with hypotension, check glucose, and call for help early. In suspected sepsis many UK hospitals use the 'Sepsis Six' bundle (oxygen, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate and urine output monitoring) with a short time window, and current NICE guidance recommends rapid treatment for high-risk patients. Always check drug choice, dose and timing against the current BNF, NICE guidance and the local sepsis pathway.

rows: Head-tilt chin-lift or jaw thrust, suction, oxygen, call emergency team
Breathing: low SpO2 or fast rate
Sit upright, oxygen to target, chest examination, blood gas and radiograph
Intravenous access, bloods and lactate, fluid bolus, look for source of bleeding or sepsis
Senior or critical care outreach review
Check glucose, airway, oxygen and review drug chart for sedatives
Urgent senior review and imaging if indicated
blocks.caption: Treat as you find: the ABCDE approach in outline.
A fluid bolus is a volume given over a short time; convert minutes to hours before dividing. Check the prescribed volume and time against current guidance.

points: Use trends in the vital signs, the track-and-trigger score and your clinical judgement together; escalate whenever you are worried.
NEWS2 is a sum of item scores with bands 0 to 4, 5 to 6 and 7 or more, plus an urgent trigger for any single 3; MAP is approximately (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3.
SBAR ends with a clear recommendation; confirm the plan and document it.

While awaiting help, treat problems as found by ABCDE, with oxygen to target, access, fluids, antibiotics as indicated and tests; always check doses and pathways against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A normal blood pressure excludes serious deterioration in a young adult who is breathing fast and has a high pulse.
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is a late sign because young, fit patients compensate for volume loss or sepsis by increasing heart rate and peripheral vasoconstriction, so the pressure can stay normal until they decompensate. A fast respiratory rate and pulse should still prompt assessment and escalation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes and vomiting has deep, rapid breathing. Observations: respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 98 percent on air, systolic BP 104 mmHg, pulse 124 per minute, alert, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. Using the NEWS2 chart (scale 1), calculate the aggregate score (a whole number).
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate 28 scores 3, SpO2 98 percent scores 0, air scores 0, systolic BP 104 scores 1, pulse 124 scores 2, alert scores 0 and temperature 36.4 scores 0. The sum is 3 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 6, which lies in the medium band and prompts an urgent response; the picture also fits dehydration with metabolic acidosis, so check glucose and ketones.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 86/48 mmHg. Using MAP = (systolic + 2 x diastolic) / 3, calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Substituting gives (86 + 2 x 48) / 3 = (86 + 96) / 3 = 182 / 3, which is about 60.7 mmHg. This is a low perfusion pressure and, in the context of an unwell patient, should prompt urgent assessment for shock and senior help.

questions.stem: During an SBAR call, which statement belongs in the Assessment section?

options.text: 'Please come and see him within 15 minutes.'
'He was admitted three days ago with a chest infection.'
'Respiratory rate 28, SpO2 91 percent on 4 litres, pulse 124, I think he has severe pneumonia.'
'I am the F1 on ward 7 calling about bed 12.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'Respiratory rate 28, SpO2 91 percent on 4 litres, pulse 124, I think he has severe pneumonia.'

distractorRationale.c: Correct: current findings and your impression of severity.

questions.explanation: The Assessment is the part of SBAR where you give the clinical findings, the early warning score and your impression of how sick the patient is. The request belongs in the Recommendation, the history belongs in Background and the introduction belongs in the Situation.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman, 3 days after hip hemiarthroplasty, is newly confused. Her respiratory rate is 28 per minute, SpO2 is 89 percent on 4 litres per minute by nasal cannulae, pulse 124 per minute and irregular, BP 88/50 mmHg and temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius. She has coarse crackles at the right base. Calculate her NEWS2 and write the SBAR you would give to the medical registrar.
markingGuide: Calculates NEWS2: respiratory rate 3, SpO2 3, oxygen 2, systolic BP 3, pulse 2, new confusion 3, temperature 1, total 17 (high risk, emergency response)
Situation: identifies self, ward, patient and the problem (acutely unwell with hypotension, hypoxia and confusion)
Background: hip hemiarthroplasty three days ago, relevant comorbidity, current medicines and escalation status

Assessment: gives the full set of observations and score, findings (right basal crackles) and impression (probable sepsis from hospital-acquired pneumonia with new fast irregular pulse, possible atrial fibrillation) and actions already taken (oxygen, ECG, access, bloods, cultures, lactate, fluids per local protocol)
Recommendation: asks for immediate senior review within a stated time, consideration of critical care outreach, and agrees a plan; reads back and documents
Doses and pathways stated as per local protocol, not invented
questions.explanation: The vignette is internally consistent: fever, new confusion, tachypnoea, hypoxia, hypotension and crackles point to sepsis with respiratory source, and a new irregular tachycardia is a common accompaniment. Marks go for a correct NEWS2 sum and a structured call that ends with a time-bound request.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has suspected sepsis with a blood pressure of 84/50 mmHg and a high lactate. While waiting for the registrar, which set of actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Give oxygen to the target range, obtain intravenous access and blood cultures, start a fluid bolus and intravenous antibiotics per the local sepsis pathway, and call for senior help
Give oral antibiotics and recheck in four hours
Give a diuretic to improve her urine output
Wait for the blood culture result before giving any antibiotic

questions.correctOptionText: Give oxygen to the target range, obtain intravenous access and blood cultures, start a fluid bolus and intravenous antibiotics per the local sepsis pathway, and call for senior help

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aligns with the sepsis bundle and early escalation; verify details locally.
distractorRationale.b: Inadequate route and delay in a hypotensive patient.
distractorRationale.c: Inappropriate in hypotension and probable hypovolaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Delays time-critical antibiotics in suspected septic shock.

questions.explanation: In suspected sepsis with hypotension, early recognition and treatment improve outcome, and bundles such as the Sepsis Six combine oxygen, cultures, intravenous antibiotics and fluid, lactate and urine output monitoring. Cultures should be taken without delaying antibiotics, and exact drugs, doses and time targets must be checked against the current BNF, NICE guidance and the local pathway.

questions.stem: A prescription asks for a 500 mL crystalloid bolus to be given over 15 minutes (check against current guidance and local policy). What infusion rate does this correspond to, in mL per hour?
questions.explanation: Convert 15 minutes to 0.25 hour, then rate equals volume divided by time: 500 mL / 0.25 h = 2000 mL per hour. This is much faster than a maintenance rate, so a bolus is given with the patient monitored and reassessed for response and signs of overload.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with sepsis is taking bisoprolol, a beta-blocker. His observations are pulse 92 per minute, blood pressure 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute and new confusion. How should his pulse of 92 be interpreted?

options.text: As proof that he does not have sepsis
As a sign that the pulse oximeter probe is faulty
As potentially falsely reassuring, because the beta-blocker can blunt the expected tachycardia, so the other findings should drive escalation
As evidence that he is haemodynamically stable

questions.correctOptionText: As potentially falsely reassuring, because the beta-blocker can blunt the expected tachycardia, so the other findings should drive escalation

distractorRationale.a: Sepsis can occur without tachycardia, especially on beta-blockers.
distractorRationale.b: Not supported by the stem; no reason to doubt the pulse.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the hypotension, tachypnoea and confusion indicate severe illness despite the pulse.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong because the blood pressure is low and the other signs are abnormal.

questions.explanation: Beta-blockers limit the heart rate response to shock, so a pulse in the 90s can coexist with significant hypovolaemia or sepsis. The hypotension, fast breathing and new confusion are far more reliable here and mean he should be treated and escalated as a high-risk patient.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man on the ward, 2 days after a knee replacement, is found drowsy. His respiratory rate is 7 per minute, SpO2 is 89 percent on air, pulse 62 per minute, BP 118/72 mmHg, pupils are small and he is on a regular opioid by a patient-controlled device. Describe your immediate assessment and first-line treatment while you call for help.
markingGuide: Calls for help (emergency team or senior) early and says why: respiratory depression
Airway: opens with simple manoeuvres and suctions if necessary
Breathing: gives oxygen and supports ventilation with a bag-valve-mask if breathing is inadequate
Recognises opioid toxicity as the likely cause (small pupils, low respiratory rate, drowsiness) and stops or pauses further opioid
Considers naloxone titrated to effect with dose and monitoring according to the BNF and local protocol, noting that its effect may wear off sooner than the opioid so observation continues
Checks capillary glucose and other causes of reduced consciousness
Documents and hands over with monitoring plan
questions.explanation: Reduced respiratory rate, small pupils and drowsiness in a patient on an opioid fit opioid-induced respiratory depression. The key is to support ventilation, remove the cause and use a reversal agent carefully, checking doses against the BNF, while calling for senior help.

questions.stem: A nurse calls you about a patient with respiratory rate 24 per minute, new confusion and systolic BP 98 mmHg, in suspected infection. How many qSOFA criteria are met, and what does this suggest?

options.text: Three criteria are met, indicating a higher risk of a poor outcome and the need for urgent senior review and treatment of possible sepsis
None are met because qSOFA needs a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius
Two criteria are met, so no escalation is needed
One criterion is met, so continue routine observations

questions.correctOptionText: Three criteria are met, indicating a higher risk of a poor outcome and the need for urgent senior review and treatment of possible sepsis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation and SBP 100 or less.
distractorRationale.b: Temperature is not part of qSOFA.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong count and wrong action: all three apply and two or more is already concerning.

questions.explanation: qSOFA counts respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation and systolic pressure of 100 mmHg or less, and this patient meets all three. A count of 2 or more flags a higher risk of poor outcome in suspected infection and should prompt urgent assessment, although qSOFA is a prompt rather than a diagnosis and local tools take precedence.
